Sides
sidz
n. pl. (the flanks or parts of a thing; the innermost recesses; rendering Hebrew tsad and yerekah)
From the Saxon side. The KJV's sides often renders Hebrew yerekah, which means the far parts or recesses — the hinder or innermost region — so that the sides of a ship or of the north are its depths rather than its edges.

Biblical Definition

Sides in the Authorized Version frequently means not edges but far recesses, and the difference matters. In the tabernacle it is plain and structural: “thou shalt put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark, that the ark may be borne with them” (Exodus 25:14). In the household psalm it is a picture of ordered blessing: “Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table” (Psalm 128:3) — the vine trained along the inner walls, fruitfulness within the home rather than displayed outside it. In Jonah it is the hold of a ship: while the mariners cried every man to his god and threw the cargo overboard, “Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep” (Jonah 1:5). The prophet is furthest in and furthest down, asleep through a storm that his own disobedience raised, while pagans pray. And Isaiah records the most famous sides in Scripture, in the boast of the king of Babylon: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13). He aims at the innermost place of the divine assembly, and the passage answers him: yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

Webster 1828 Definition

The flanks — and in the KJV often the innermost recesses. A wife fruitful by the sides of the house, Jonah asleep in the sides of the ship, and a king aiming at the sides of the north who is brought to the sides of the pit.

expand to see more

SIDE, n. [Sax. side.] The broad or long surface of a body, as distinguished from the end, which is of less extent.

2. Margin; edge; verge; border; the exterior line of any thing.

3. The part between the top and bottom; the slope; declivity; as the side of a hill.

4. Party; faction; interest; as, he took our side in the dispute.

5. In Scripture, the inner or hinder parts; the sides of the north, Is. 14; the sides of the pit, Is. 14.

Key Scripture

Exodus 25:14 — "And thou shalt put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark, that the ark may be borne with them."

Psalm 128:3 — "Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table."

Jonah 1:5 — "Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep."

Isaiah 14:13 — "For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:"

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 14 is read as a merely political taunt, losing the pattern of prideful ascent it exposes — and Psalm 128's picture of fruitfulness centred in the home is treated as a diminishment of women.

expand to see more

Isaiah 14:13-14 is a five-fold I will — I will ascend, I will exalt, I will sit, I will ascend above the heights, I will be like the most High — and it names the anatomy of pride wherever it appears. Whether the taunt is aimed only at a Babylonian king or reaches behind him to the fall of Lucifer, the pattern is the same and the answer is the same: the ascent ends in the sides of the pit. Reading the passage as ancient political rhetoric and nothing more removes the mirror it was meant to be. Every self-exaltation follows the same five steps and arrives at the same address. Psalm 128:3 is likewise resented, because a wife described as a fruitful vine by the sides of the house sounds to modern ears like confinement. The image is of honour, not restriction: the vine is the most valued planting a household had, trained where it would flourish, and its fruit was the family's wealth. Scripture's ordering of the home is creational, and it dignifies what it orders.

The principle to recover is Jonah in the hold. The sides of the ship are the deepest and most sheltered place aboard, and that is exactly where a fleeing prophet is found asleep while unbelieving sailors pray for their lives. Disobedience does not usually feel like a storm; it feels like sleep in a quiet place, several decks below the trouble one has caused. The shipmaster's question is the sermon — What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God — and it had to be put to the prophet by a heathen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsad is a side or flank; yerekah is the far or innermost part — the recesses of a ship, a cave, or the north. Greek pleura is the side of the body.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsad (H6654) — a side, a flank; the ordinary word for the side of a thing or person.

Hebrew yerekah (H3411) — the far parts, recesses, hinder region; the sides of the north and of the pit.

Hebrew tsela (H6763) — a rib, a side; the side chambers of the temple and the rib taken from Adam.

Greek pleura (G4125) — the side of the body; the side of Christ pierced with a spear.

Greek meros (G3313) — a part, a portion, a side; the parts and coasts of a region.

Usage

"Of the staves borne at the ark's sides: put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark (Exodus 25:14)."

"Of fruitfulness within the home: thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house (Psalm 128:3)."

"Of pride's highest aim: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north (Isaiah 14:13)."
